identification.summary: Earth Wendigo is a Trend Micro-named threat actor that has targeted Taiwanese government organizations, research institutions and universities since May 2019, using JavaScript injected into a widely used Taiwanese webmail system to exfiltrate email [S1][S2]. Trend Micro found no clear connection to previously known attack groups and named the actor itself [S2]. Trend Micro also observed separate spear-phishing emails with malicious links sent to politicians and activists who support Tibet, the Uyghur region or Hong Kong, which it treated as a distinct series of attacks [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: 2019-05 (start of the Taiwan webmail campaign per Trend Micro) [S1][S2].
identification.notes: The Google Drive spear-phishing results that surfaced in searches belong to a different Trend Micro cluster (Earth Preta) and must not be merged with Earth Wendigo. The webmail product is not named in the retrieved summaries.

attribution.confidence: Trend Micro named the actor itself because it saw no clear connection to earlier groups [S2]. No state attribution was confirmed in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Trend Micro January 2021 research [S1]. No sponsoring organization or country is named in the sources gathered.

objectives: Email theft from Taiwanese government, research and university targets [S1][S2]. The Tibet, Uyghur and Hong Kong lures suggest interest in individuals associated with those causes [S1]; the sources gathered do not state a sponsor or tasking.

sectors: Politicians and activists (Tibet, Uyghur region, Hong Kong causes)
targeting.notes: The politician and activist targeting was reported by Trend Micro as separate from the Taiwan webmail operation [S1][S2].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing emails posing as a shopping-coupon ad carry hidden obfuscated JavaScript, triggered through the webmail search-suggestion feature to evade static checks [S2][S5]. The primary route is XSS injection into the webmail system; if that fails, the actor registers a malicious script as a Service Worker, which can intercept and manipulate HTTPS requests, hijack login credentials and add malicious scripts to the webmail page [S1][S5]. The final-stage backdoor opens a WebSocket channel; its single command, get('URL'), makes the victim's browser request a URL from the webmail server and return the response, which lets the server read email and attachments [S5][S2]. Related scripts stole cookies and webmail session keys and spread via victims' email signatures [S2]. Trend Micro reported the XSS flaw was fixed in January 2020, so only unpatched servers remained exposed [S2]. Python malware compiled as Windows executables was found to be shellcode loaders for code likely Cobalt Strike [S5].

diamond.adversary: Unnamed actor tracked by Trend Micro as Earth Wendigo; no sponsor stated in sources [S2].
diamond.capability: XSS injection into webmail, Service Worker persistence, WebSocket-driven browser-side email theft, obfuscated JavaScript lures, Python Cobalt Strike-style loaders [S2][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Attacker servers delivering follow-on scripts and a WebSocket server directing the victim browser [S2][S5]; specific domains and IPs not captured here.
diamond.victim: Taiwanese government, research institutions and universities; separately politicians and activists tied to Tibet, Uyghur region and Hong Kong causes [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Email collection against Taiwanese institutions and Tibet/Uyghur/Hong Kong supporters; no sponsor stated in sources.
diamond.technology: Unpatched webmail with an XSS flaw, and browser Service Worker capability, which let the actor persist and read mail from inside the victim's authenticated session [S2][S5].

gaps: Trend Micro's report was not opened directly (fetch failed); details come from search-result summaries of it and from SecurityWeek/Cyble coverage that was not individually fetched [S1][S5].
The webmail product is not named in the retrieved material.
No aliases or MITRE ATT&CK group ID found; no Microsoft name mapping checked.
No activity after January 2021 found in the searches run.
Overlap with other China-nexus clusters was not assessed by Trend Micro per the retrieved text [S2].
No state or country attribution was confirmed; earlier aggregator (Malpedia/MISP) China labels could not be verified and were removed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Browser-accessed webmail and the user sessions inside it are key terrain; Taiwanese government and academic mail holds the target data [S1][S2]. STEP 2: The actor exploited a known webmail XSS that was patched in January 2020, so unpatched web applications are the exposed seam [S2]. STEP 3: Template is lure email, then XSS or Service Worker, then WebSocket browser proxy, then bulk mail retrieval from inside the authenticated session, which leaves little endpoint malware [S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued email collection against Taiwanese public-sector and academic organizations. MDCOA, speculative and not stated in sources, would be the same technique against allied or coalition webmail used during a Taiwan contingency. Candidate indicators: unexpected Service Worker registrations on webmail origins, WebSocket connections from webmail pages to unfamiliar hosts, obfuscated script in search-suggestion or signature fields [S2][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track web-application patch status for any webmail used by partner or coalition staff; the reported flaw was an old, fixed vulnerability [S2]. (2) Authorities: browser-side email theft occurs on partner or host-nation systems, so coordination runs through the owning organization, not US-controlled networks. (3) Mission assurance: treat webmail as untrusted for sensitive planning traffic where webmail patching cannot be verified. (4) Coordination: share indicators such as Service Worker and WebSocket anomalies with partner CERTs; attribution is unsettled, so prioritize detection over naming.

provenance.importedSummary: Earth Wendigo is a threat actor from China that has been targeting several organizations — including government organizations, research institutions, and universities in Taiwan — since May 2019, aiming to exfiltrate emails from targeted organizations via the injection of JavaScript backdoors to a webmail system that is widely used in Taiwan. The threat actor also sent spear-phishing emails embedded with malicious links to multiple individuals, including politicians and activists, who support movements in Tibet, the Uyghur region, or Hong Kong.
